lines.text: Every broken checkout costs a sale. A customer adds three mugs, the cart says eighteen dollars instead of fifty-four, and they leave.
Bugs like this ship because the tests pass, and nobody clicks through the whole journey. And coding agents say done the moment their tests go green.
CheckoutGuard changes who decides. Not the agent. A real browser.
First, Kane CLI tests the checkout in real Chrome, step by step, like a customer. When something's wrong, it fails the journey, and explains why.
That evidence goes to a coding agent, boxed in: its own copy of the code, no shell, no web, and no way to touch the tests.
Then Kane runs the exact same journey again. If it passes, the fix is verified. If it fails, it stays a failure, however confident the agent is.
And nothing merges by itself. A person reviews the change, and approves it.
On our demo store, Kane caught all three seeded checkout bugs. The agent fixed all three, and Kane verified every fix.
CheckoutGuard. Every checkout tested. Every fix verified.
